title: IFNA: catch only a missing match

screens.prompt: In B9, look the code in A8 up in the table and say not on the list when it is missing.

hints.syntax: =IFNA(VLOOKUP(A8,A2:B7,2,FALSE),"not on the list") — the fallback is the second argument.
hints.func-ifna: A lookup that finds nothing needs a replacement for #N/A, and only #N/A.
hints.func-vlookup: The price sits in the second column of the table, so a lookup is the shortest route.
hints.require-ref: Look the code up from the cell instead of typing Q-9 into the formula.
hints.value: Q-9 is not in the code column, so the fallback is the answer.
hints.error: IFNA replaces #N/A only; a #REF! from a wrong column comes through untouched.

screens.prompt: In B9, price the code in A2 with the same lookup, keeping the fallback for a missing code.

hints.syntax: =IFNA(VLOOKUP(A2,A2:B7,2,FALSE),"not on the list") — the fallback stays even when the lookup works.
hints.func-ifna: The guard belongs in the formula even on a row that happens to be found.
hints.func-vlookup: The price is the second column of the table.
hints.require-ref: Read the code from the grid so the answer follows the row.
hints.value: A-1 is the first row of the table, so its price of 10 is returned.
hints.error: A #DIV/0! from outside the lookup is not #N/A, so IFNA passes it straight through.

reject.why: the lookup is unguarded, so a code that is not on the list would show an error
the first column returns the code A-1 instead of the price
a different range is searched, so the code in the grid is never read
an index and match finds the row, but this lesson asks for the lookup function itself
the table has two columns, so the column number is out of range and #REF! escapes IFNA
the found price is then divided by zero
the missing comma inside VLOOKUP breaks the argument list

docs.explain: IFNA is IFERROR with a narrower net. It evaluates its first argument and, if that argument fails with #N/A — the error a lookup raises when it finds no match — returns the second argument instead. Any other error, and there are several, passes straight through: a #REF! from a column number that does not exist, a #VALUE! from text in arithmetic, a #DIV/0! from an empty divisor all survive IFNA and land in the cell. That narrowness is the point. Wrapping a lookup in IFERROR hides a broken range or a misspelled column behind the same friendly word that hides an ordinary miss, and the sheet then reports no match for a formula that has a bug. IFNA keeps the two apart: missing data says so, broken formulas still shout. In this drill Q-9 is not in the code column, so the first screen returns the fallback while the second looks up A-1, finds 10, and never reaches its fallback at all. Both screens keep the guard in place, because the point of a guard is the row that has not been typed yet. Nothing about IFNA changes the value when the lookup succeeds: it returns exactly what it was handed.

errors.text: The error IFNA exists to replace, raised by a lookup or a match that found nothing.
A column or row number outside the range; IFNA does not catch this.
Text used where a number was needed; IFNA does not catch this either.

docs.atWork: Pricing an order line from a product table and printing no match instead of a broken lookup.
docs.outcome: Replace a missing lookup match without hiding the other errors in the formula.
